newsitem.title: JAPAN: World biggest nuclear site worries smalltown Japan.
newsitem.headline: World biggest nuclear site worries smalltown Japan.

text.p: The start-up of Japan's 51st commercial reactor on Wednesday will make a nuclear power plant in northern Japan the world's largest.
But not everyone is cheering, the region's local officials say, with residents of the small, coastal communities near the plant voicing renewed concerns about the disposal of used nuclear fuel.

"Given the fact that used nuclear fuel is piling up in the power plant with no place to go, I'm not in the mood to celebrate the number-one status," said Kazuyuki Takemoto, a town assembly member in Kariwamura on the Sea of Japan coast.
Tokyo Electric Power Co Inc (TEPCO) plans to start commercial operation of a 1.36 million kilowatt (kw) reactor at its Kashiwazaki-Kariwa nuclear power complex on July 2.
The name of the plant comes from its location on the border between Kariwamura, a small farming town of 5,400 people, and the medium-sized city of Kashiwazaki.

The new reactor, the plant's seventh, will raise total power generation capacity at the plant to 8.2 million kw, which effectively dethrones Canada's 7.3-million-kw Bruce nuclear power plant in Ontario as the world's largest plant.

But a stalemate on development of Japan's key storage facility for spent nuclear fuel has residents near Kashiwazaki-Kariwa wondering whether the plant's radioactive material won't end up in their own backyard.
"I think there's a good chance that we will end up with the spent fuel permanently," Takemoto said.

The storage facility -- planned as part of a spent nuclear fuel reprocessing plant in northern Japan's Aomori prefecture -- was meant to begin receiving the discharge from Japan's nuclear industry in June.

But a string of accidents at other nuclear power sites have stalled development of the Aomori storage facility completely, leaving commercial power plants across Japan, including the Kashiwazaki-Kariwa complex, with rising stockpiles of used nuclear fuel.
"No one can force Aomori to take what they do not want," Takemoto added.
An official for the municipal government of Kashiwazaki said residents there shared the same concerns as those in Kariwamura.
"Every time we talk about nuclear issues here, the discussion boils down to the fact that problems regarding storage of spent fuel remain unsolved," he said.
"We just hope the government will do its best to bring the stalled (Aomori) talks back on track again."

The prefectural government of Aomori said talks on safety measures for the spent fuel storage facility, necessary for the plant to start accepting spent fuel, would not resume until government officials had pinpointed the cause of Japan's worst-ever nuclear accident in March.
The Science and Technology Agency, which is carrying out the probe into the cause of that accident, said it remains unclear when the investigation will be concluded.
In March, a fire and explosion at Japan's sole spent nuclear fuel reprocessing plant in Tokaimura, northeast of Tokyo, exposed 37 workers to low levels of radiation.
